articles.title: MAKE ME THEREOF A LITTLE CAKE FIRST
articles.author: G. W. Brown

paragraphs.text: I want to add a word to what we have had as to Christ and the assembly. I am thinking of the way that we are brought vitally into the appreciation of the assembly. It must be by way of revelation. Of course, there is what precedes; there is the work of the Spirit of God, which is sovereign, according to John 3, in new birth. Apart from that, there would be no power to receive any feature of the truth. It is evident that, in Peter, that work had begun. God had sovereignly wrought in him the answer to this enquiry by the Lord, “But ye, who do ye say that I am?” It was a wonderful answer that Peter gave, and it witnesses to the work of God in him, and, in addition, to the Father’s revelation.

If we turn to Luke 1: 35, the angel said to Mary, “The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, and power of the Highest overshadow thee, wherefore the holy thing also which shall be born shall be called Son of God” Now Peter says, “Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God”.

As we examine ourselves, are we conscious of having had such a revelation as to the Person, “The Christ, the Son of the living God”? The Lord recognises the Father’s movements in saying, “Flesh and blood has not revealed it to thee, but my Father”. Have we faith for it—that we have been the subjects of divine service thus—the Spirit of God bringing about what is new in us, and the Father making this revelation as to His Son? How sovereign it is—how blessed! How infinitely favoured we are to be the subjects of the Father’s revelation concerning His Son! The Lord says to Peter, in answer to this, “And I also, I say unto thee”. There is a deliberateness about it which perhaps we have not always noticed. As if the Lord would say, I am going to say something. You have said something, Peter—something you could not have said without the Father’s revelation “and I also, I say unto thee that thou art Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly, and hades’ gates shall not prevail against it”.

Here we are, at the end of the dispensation, as we most assuredly believe, and we have been speaking together, in some measure intelligibly, about the assembly—speaking of it as a present, known, reality. We say thankfully to God that we know that it finds expression in this place where we are. In this small company, despised no doubt by the world, and it may be too by others who were formerly found here with them; but we are assured that there is in this place an expression of the assembly. May it please God to add to it, and above all, to sustain it, till the coming of the Lord, which may not be long.

Here, as in other places, outwardly so reduced, and so small, there is nevertheless an expression of the assembly, that which we have spoken of as connected with the prime thoughts and counsels of God in purpose for His own pleasure, that which has the privilege of setting forth what may be known of God in this very town. What a privilege it is! What a privilege for all of us in the places to which we belong to have part in the setting forth of God as He may be known by men. As the expression of the assembly is found in each place it is contributed to by each one of us.

There is something basic in this confession of Peter, “Thou art the Christ”. Think of the volume of Jewish history that looked forward—and does still, I suppose—to the coming of Christ, the centuries of history in which Christ had been expected, not by Gentiles, but by Jews. And here is a man addressing Jesus, “Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God”. I doubt whether the second statement was understood and looked forward to in the long history of Jewish faith and expectancy. I doubt whether it was known that the One who would answer to that official title would be the Son of the living God.

The Father had made it known to Peter, and the Lord says, I have something to say, “Thou art Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly”—that is, on the knowledge of Himself as revealed by the Father in the hearts of men—in our hearts—“and hades’ gates shall not prevail against it”. Here, at the end of the dispensation, on the eve of the rapture, there is the expression of the assembly in so many places, despite the unfaithfulness that has marked us all; despite the divisions, alas, amongst the most favoured saints, who have been in the light of recovered truth for the past 150 years approximately. Now, on the eve of the rapture, the truth of the assembly is found in expression in smallness. How fitting it seems that it should be in smallness, in view of the failure on man’s side; but it is preserved in vitality and power by the Spirit of God and by the blessed Lord Himself.

I read from 1 Kings and it might be wondered how this connects with what we have been considering, but again it seems fitting that the person referred to should be in these circumstances of weakness and poverty, almost of desperation. The brethren no doubt recall ministry about it years ago, as to how well it might describe a local company. A widow woman was there gathering sticks. Her natural resource had gone. Her occupation was something very lowly, but the prophet comes to where she is. The prophet is he who represents God in His rights. We might say that he represents the Lord Jesus. The prophet makes request to the woman.

This is not the gospel. God is not requesting anything of man in the gospel—He is supplying it all. I hope we preach that! If you preach a gospel in which God is supplying everything, you will have grounds to invite men to repent so that they may receive all the blessing. But do present first the resources that are with God to save, and to deliver, man—all the resources that are in Christ. As I say, in the gospel God is not requiring anything from man; He is supplying it.

This is the Lord in His dealings, we may say, with a company. Maybe they are reduced to extremity; the position weak and despicable to the natural mind—a widow gathering sticks. But the prophet makes a request of her, “Fetch me, I pray thee, a little water in a vessel, that I may drink”. Do we rise above our own weakness to think of the Lord? I think we do. We do, at least, once a week as we assemble for the Supper, thinking of the Lord—something for Him.

Then it says “she went to fetch it”—a very good feature that. In spite of her adversity she is obedient. Then he makes another request, “And he called to her and said, Bring me, I pray thee, a morsel of bread in thy hand”. He does not ask for a lot—a morsel of bread. Then she says, I cannot do that. At the best I have just a handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse. I have just got the bare necessities for this last meal for me and my son—we are giving up. The position is hopeless; we are about to give up. We are just going to use what little we have left for ourselves. We will survive until that has gone, and then all will be finished. Ever felt like that? Maybe—the Lord knows. “That I may go in and dress it for me and my son, that we may eat it and die”.

Elijah said to her, “Fear not”. Maybe the Lord is Speaking to ourselves in this, “Fear not; go, do as thou hast said; but make me thereof a little cake first”—the emphasis is on first; “me … first”. If the position is weak, and we are getting desperate, dear brethren, the remedy is to think of the Lord first. The little cake is a reference, typically, to the assembly. The intention to use what little is left “for me and my son” as a last meal before finally giving up is what we are prone to, I think, as lacking in faith in the power of the Spirit and in the love of Christ.

I suppose many of us would confess to that, feeling that things are too much, that the end is in sight—not God’s end, but the end for unbelief. It is lack of faith in the Spirit and in the love of Christ.

However, the word of the prophet is sufficient and she follows it. “Bring it to me; and afterwards make for thee and for thy son”. Let us keep it before us, beloved brethren, however weak the position may be, that the Son of God who has been revealed to us is to be ministered to. He is to have something to drink; He is to have this little cake. We have enough for that; what is of Christ in us, and the power of the Spirit, in the oil—and the oil was in a cruse, in a vessel. What is causing the leakage, you see, is self; we are thinking of self—maybe self in all its weakness; Is the Son of the living God going to fail us? Is He going to desert us? Or are we going to consider, when in ourselves we are so deplorably weak, for Him, that He may drink—and that He may have what is represented in this little cake; something for Himself? He said to Peter, “I will build my assembly, and hades’ gates shall not prevail against it”. We might say that, typically, through the activity of the prophet here, he ensured that hades’ gates did not prevail, for it says that “she, and he, and her house, ate a whole year”. It suggests an extended period, until the Lord comes.

It is not the end of exercise because afterwards there is defection in the household, as there may be in a locality. There may be defection in any one of us. The best brother in the meeting may prove to be defective. If Paul said that he needed to buffet his body, and lead it captive, lest having preached to others he should be himself rejected (1 Corinthians 9: 27), surely there is no one amongst us who does not need to do it.

The son died; then she is cast back on herself. She says, “Art thou come to me to call mine iniquity to remembrance?” The Son of God does not go back, like we do. Thank God for that We are in danger of going back. The epistle to the Hebrews shows that. Do not let us say, That is just Hebrews; that is not us. God has provided in the word, and in the Spirit, for everything that might arise amongst us, and one of the things that might arise is a going back.

Let us face it. Let us not say, Not me! We have said that long enough. Whoever would have thought, haw inconceivable it was, say twenty years ago, that things should have come to the pass they did publicly in the testimony—the shameful things amongst us. Do not let us say again, That is not us. Do not let anyone say, That is not me. How easily we go back, but for divine grace. I am not speaking about one’s final destiny—that is assured; nothing can shake it. I am thinking about the course of the testimony. How many mighty men have fallen; they are out of it; they have perished in the wilderness. What sort of people were they who perished in the wilderness? Well, they included princes—and princesses, I suppose—the last sort of people that you would have thought would perish, belonging to a nation as to which God had such purposes of blessing.

You would have said, Well, they will get through—they will surely get through. They perished in the wilderness! Many have done so in this dispensation. Many who have preached to others have themselves been rejected. I do not want to depress the brethren; I want to strengthen myself and my brethren in confidence in the Son of God and in the way that we shall be preserved in vitality as we change our outlook from self to God and to Christ.

However desperate the situation may seem to be, let us not be thinking of ourselves, but of what is of and for Christ, peculiarly what has the character of the assembly—“but make me … a little cake first”. The man of God was equal to the situation, and the moment came when he said to the widow; “See, thy son lives”. It is a matter, here in type, which has occurred and recurred, and it may be there will be more recurrence before the rapture in many localities. Christ is equal to the situation. Our salvation will be in considering not for ourselves, but for Him. May it be so, for His name’s sake.

The challenge ofttimes of the recovery must of necessity be deep, for in times of recovery God carries through what is of Himself, despite what may seem to have overcome it, what may seem to have overcome it. Soon we shall be in a scene and circumstances where no adverse thing shall ever come. The Spirit is able to sustain in us some conception of that—the scene and circumstances in which no adverse thing shall be. And yet we have to realise that what is adverse is with us yet. Not, however, without the availability and perfect efficacy of provision to meet every adversity. What a comfort it is, with the deep searchings of the present time with us, to realise that God is able to carry through everything which He loves to call attention to as being of Himself. He is doing that. But yet the scripture shows us clearly that the recovery involves persons by whom God effects what He is doing.

So in this man Nehemiah we have remarkable circumstances presented to us, first that God had intervened sovereignly from His side. The intervention initially is not in the book of Nehemiah, it is in the book of Ezra, which precedes, when God brought it into the heart of a Gentile ruler, Cyrus, to effect something in regard of what God had in view concerning Jerusalem—God came in.

I believe it right for us to remind ourselves at the present time that, 150 years ago approximately, God came in. That was not of man; it was of God. In certain respects the way in which things proceeded was not always marked by entire correspondence at every point; but the intervention was of God. It is good for us to reflect on that; to get back to it; God did that thing. Not that I want, today, to go over history or to make specific reference to particular persons, although God used particular persons; but God came in to effect something that was in His mind to be for the carrying through to finality of what was, and is, in His own mind. It was in His mind, and it is in His mind, because divine thoughts do not change. It was in His mind, and it is in His mind, to carry through what is of Himself to a point of finality.

Then there arose men like Ezra, Zerubbabel, Joshua or Jeshua, men of great worth that God used, and a point of recovery was reached, a house was set up for service, the service was provided for, and yet, alas, things fell back, to a certain point at least, for loss of impetus. We have to search out our own times and our own course as to that. So Mr. Darby refers in the notes in the beginning of 2 Timothy to a certain condition of things that called for stimulation, for stirring, for the reviving to the real spirit and character of what God was doing.

Have we not needed that, dear brethren? Is it not a sobering consideration to realise that, maybe as to ourselves, the impetus for things was lost? Elements of decline so quickly creep in—I speak feelingly, I know it in my own heart—elements of decline, at least to the extent of lack of devoted energy, come in. We need reviving. And God loves to see a reviving. He will bring about a reviving today as we hearken to His voice. I go back to times of earlier history—and we have sometimes to speak of our own experience and realise that when we are younger things often go, as men say, by fits and starts. You get a touch and you live on it for a little while and then, alas, things drift back a bit, and the Lord in His faithfulness gives you another touch. How faithful He is! Oh, the faithfulness of Christ!—the divine faithfulness we experience, especially early in our histories, but all the way through our histories.

You young ones here, have you not proved the faithfulness of God; that He abides faithful? It is simple to say that the very fact that you are here today is a reflection of the faithfulness of God. Have regard to that. Speak to Him simply about it—the way He has gone on in His faithfulness with you, just that you may come into the fulness of what He delights to revive.
Oh the wonder of it that any one of us is here today! Let us realise the faithfulness, the divine faithfulness, the mercy, that enter into that—God coming in from His side.

So what we find in Nehemiah is that God had a man in whom He signally wrought, and, you know, a man is needed. I just seek to bring out that point, that God has thoughts in His mind and He works them out as having a man that He can work on, and a man who is ready to stand in what He is doing. Here in Nehemiah it was just one man, and save for that passing reference to certain men that went with Him, in the second chapter, the concern of this is all his, Nehemiah’s. As the matter opens out he is not looking for support from anyone, basically, save from God.

Well, we have to come back to this, and maybe we have been wayward in getting back to it; but the point of help all the way through is from God. We try to depend on other supposed resources of help—what have they proved to be? The great resource of help is from God. He has the means that He uses. The full way of divine provisions is within range of His use; the gifts that He has established and used; the men whom He has established in right leadership and used in right leadership. All those have their place; but the basis of help is with God.
The simplicity of Nehemiah’s prayer is to be taken note of, “Let now thine ear be attentive to the prayer of thy servant, and to the prayer of thy servants who delight to fear thy name”.

That is, Nehemiah is not entirely alone, in the sense that there are in his mind others. They are not seen as joining with him, but he is not leaving out those who, as he says, delight to fear God’s name. For we find that, though they may not be directly and immediately available, as we go on with God there are others who go on with God. There are others who go on with God. The point is not developed here in Nehemiah because the Spirit’s point in this book is to call attention to the exercise of this one man.

But what are my exercises about the testimony? What are my concerns? What are my prayers for the testimony? And if I may be personal and definite about it, what are yours? Is there anything formed in you in concern for the prospering of what God is doing in view of a glorious finish? Is my mind or heart empty of concern in respect of divine interests? I ask myself that. It would not be so, I judge, with any person here; but it might be. Is my mind empty, my heart empty, my prayers empty, of what relates to the full scope of divine interests?

Here is a man who is simple, brief, definite as he speaks to God, and feeling as he speaks to God. You might say you have remarkable elements of prayer in this single verse. Here is a man who has power with God and you see, even in this single verse, something of the basis of the power he had with God, the simplicity of the man, the definiteness of the man, and the committedness of the man. “Let now thine ear be attentive to the prayer of thy servant, and to the prayer of thy servants who delight to fear thy name”. “Thy servant”—the lowly place he takes, God’s servant. What a God to serve: What a God we have to serve; but are we content just to take and accept and fill out the servant’s place, involving, as this does, all that we have been remarking about the recognition of authority in Christ, and all that we have been saying as to the workings of headship amongst us? But the servant’s place is to be known, and accepted by us; but what a God to serve!

“And prosper, I pray thee, thy servant this day, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man”. That is, the immediate circumstances are in his mind. We keep in touch with the immediate circumstances. God gives grace and wisdom and resource in the immediate circumstances.

We might wish them other than they are; clearly Nehemiah would have preferred circumstances other than those in which he was, but he accepts the circumstances perfectly, and God blesses him on that basis.

You see, we might be fretful in circumstances. Maybe that there are particular concerns as to the place where God has set me. Maybe there are very few available in the place where God has set me. We might easily be fretful in those circumstances. We feel the circumstances; God would have us to feel them, and yet this man just accepts the circumstances and seeks, as he says, “Prosper, I pray thee, thy servant this day”. As if he says, if I may put a certain point into it, Thine interests are paramount. Here am I, and if no one else be available, I will be in Thy hand. What a point to come to! But it relates to what God delights to revive and to carry through; not only that His interests go through, but His interests go through in suitability to Himself by means of those who are committed in a feeling, intelligent way to what He is doing.
I read that second passage just to touch this fine point which is in it, “I told no man what my God had put in my heart to do for Jerusalem”. That, to me, is a wonderful section of scripture,

“I told no man what my God had put in my heart to do for Jerusalem”. It shows the view that is with this man—Jerusalem. What does he see? Ruin. He goes out at night. What night we are in as to anything in the public relations of what can be spoken of as christendom. What a night it is. And if we go out and conduct what we might speak of as a tour of inspection, what shall we find? As he says, “ruins, and its gates were consumed with fire”. Is he depressed? Is he overcome? No. He goes forward, he labours, he stimulates others to labour, he uses strong methods to stimulate them sometimes, as the end of the book shows; but he goes forward, committed on the basis of depth of conviction in himself as to the God of whom he speaks as my God, and convicted as to what he knows his God would have him do.

So he goes forward, but let us note, dear brethren, it is, as he says, “for Jerusalem”. It is not the personal prowess of Nehemiah that is in mind to be celebrated. It is not that they are to make deductions about Nehemiah that attach certain fame to him. Have you any personal motives in going forward in the testimony, of any kind whatsoever? Am I seeking, in any manner, mere personal advantage in what is proceeding? We have to face these things; not that I am accusing anybody of such base motives, but we have to search these things out. It is “for Jerusalem”. Though they be few with whom our relations closely and locally may stand, what is in our hearts is Jerusalem—the whole assembly, the full answer to the divine thoughts, the full answer to them. A city, Jerusalem, is presented to us as a complete, intact thought.

The enemy would rob us of that in relation to the assembly, and use every means and every conflict and every experience, if possible, to rob us of the entire and intact thought of what the assembly is in relation to Christ, and what that vessel is in the divine thoughts. It is “for Jerusalem”. There is nothing in this book to minister to what we speak of as independence—nothing. The labour is “for Jerusalem”, and yet it requires you, it requires me, it requires every one of us, in full, devoted committal and readiness as need may arise to go on in suffering. The end in mind—glorious! A scene of things, as I said, where no adversity comes.
In the course of what proceeds towards that great end the service of the Spirit brings in so much related to the glory of Christ for the present sustaining of true hearts.

So as Timothy went on with Paul how much he would constantly derive in Paul’s company of present satisfaction in the knowledge of the love of Christ as he saw it in Paul and as he experienced it in the circle in which Paul moved. I am speaking now of this that we may understand, as God would give us to understand, the present compensations. We are enjoying them today—I am, anyway—the present compensations. I do not set myself apart in saying that, but I say it in that sense because it is a question of reality in what every one of us is going through in experience, and what I find today is present compensation in the circle of those who love Christ, in the sense of fulness in our relations with Christ, and the sense of realisation of what the Spirit is to us in going through to the finish in the scene that is so adverse to Him.

Present compensation!—I am assured that Timothy had it in the company of Paul. I am assured that the Lord will constantly furnish it to faithful persons; a sense of present compensation in the realisation of a faithful love that knows no limit, and the experience of a circle in which that love is valued and enhanced to us in all its wealth and its power. Dear young people, go on in the realisation that the Lord will give you present compensation. It may not be in circumstances of an agreeable kind; it will be in the intimacy of your own relations in secret with Himself, and your own relations in the assembly with those amongst whom the Lord delights to come—present compensation. I would be failing in speaking of a course of things in time, in view of revival, if I did not call attention to that positive side of what the present activity of the unfailing love of Christ for the assembly furnishes to those who seek to stand in faithfulness to what the assembly for Himself involves on our side.

So that in speaking to Timothy and writing to Timothy at the close, attention is called by Paul to certain features—“Thou hast been thoroughly acquainted with my teaching, conduct, purpose, faith, longsuffering, love, endurance, persecutions, sufferings”. What a list of features called attention to by the apostle!—things that this young man Timothy had seen.

You know, many of us have seen such features in those whom God has used. Many of us have read of such features in those God has used. Many of us have been able to see those features working, even in the writings of those whom God has used.

But those features are to be taken on; they are to be maintained; none of them is to be allowed to lapse. They constitute the expression in love of the very recovery to which God has called His saints; the expression in love of the features that properly relate to this recovery. For the recovery is not a theory; it is not an abstraction; it is a reality in life. Would you not have your part in that? Is it not a wonderful thing to have part in, the reviving of life according to God, which leads to the presentation before Him, even, as need arises, in adverse circumstances, of what answers to Himself? And this would cover the whole extent, the whole area, of the course of the testimony. It is not just a question of times of privilege on the first day of the week (Oh, the delight of the Lord to afford us those times!) but seven days a week, twenty-four hours a day, until the Lord comes.

Paul refers later to those who love His appearing. Thank God for those who love His appearing. We love to think that what is in Christ personally is to be brought forward in His full majesty and power, and yet we are left a little moment longer, a little moment longer.

Some of us were speaking in conversation this week of every indication that the little moment is truly that. Maybe we have been saying this for many years past, but we are saying it now with greater conviction than ever before, that there is but a little moment that may remain.
And yet these features are to go through. Take them up; one by one. They finish with the point of suffering. The testimony began in suffering—the testimony will finish in suffering.

The character of the suffering is another thing. It began in suffering, it will finish in suffering; but the suffering at the beginning did not in any sense impede the sense of divine supply in which the suffering was gone through. You could see that in the early chapters of the Acts, the sense of power that came in. In Acts 4, as the suffering became acute, the place in which they were assembled shook—power from God to sustain His lovers in suffering. God will never deprive us of that. The suffering circumstances may come upon any one of us severally as the reproach of Christ is borne. It may come upon all who seek to walk in the truth, generally or in particular areas; the sufferings will come.

The testimony began in suffering; it is finishing in suffering; the sufferings are with us now; but let us see that what is going through is of God, and what is going through is divinely supplied, and this second epistle to Timothy, often referred to, and needfully before us at the present time, relates to the reviving of love and to matters going through as God would have them sustained in the vitality of what is living according to God.

Well, I do not touch on these features severally, but it impressed me this morning how God has caused these features to be set out as something that Timothy had known in Paul, and now they are to be carried forward. And it depends upon us, beloved brethren, to carry them forward. It is not pretentious to say that—it is the acceptance of what God would lay upon us—it is not pretentious. It is for us to carry forward, in living expression, features which substantially answer to what came out in the beginning in God’s beloved servant Paul, so uniquely taken up and used of Him at the start.

May we go through, dear brethren, remembering that the recovery is always to what God began when the Spirit came at Pentecost, and nothing less than that is to govern us as we go forward together. May He strengthen us for it, for His name’s sake.

articles.title: THE GLAD TIDINGS OF YOUR SALVATION
articles.author: A. A. Bellamy

paragraphs.text: I read from Ephesians because of the reference to the glad tidings. Paul, as we know, is writing to believers; he writes to “the saints and faithful in Christ Jesus who are at Ephesus” (Ephesians 1: 1), and he brings in very early this allusion to the glad tidings of their salvation.

It proves one thing at least, that the saints need the glad tidings, and we have to be specific in our thoughts of the glad tidings as presented to the saints—I mean as distinct from persons who are unbelievers. If any such were to come into this occasion, the Lord would surely speak to them. So I believe the Lord would speak to us who, like those in Ephesus, have trusted in Christ.
How simple these thoughts are that Paul speaks of in the highest of his epistles, “In whom ye also have trusted”. He begins, and we begin, with Christ, the One in whom we have trusted.

But then he says, “having heard the word of the truth, the glad tidings of your salvation”. This is very interesting because it shows that the full thought of salvation involves that we are not only to be delivered from the bondage of Egypt, and brought into the wilderness, as the people were, but we are to be brought out of the wilderness, and into the purpose of God for us as believers.

We are prone to think of God’s purpose as something to be fulfilled in the future, when we are in bodies of glory, and so it will be; but there is a side in which we can, and should, come into the realm of His purpose for us now. Therefore it is “the glad tidings of your salvation”. We know, in the history of the people of God in the wilderness, what a great matter it was to get them out of the wilderness and into the land, and there is the same reluctance with us as believers very often, not because of the claims of the world, but of nature, and all that is connected with the provisional order of God’s ways in the wilderness where, nonetheless, He may be learned, as the hymn says—

“In the desert God will teach thee
What the God that thou hast found”
But then many who came out of Egypt into the wilderness died in the wilderness; Caleb and Joshua, however, went right through. They really represent those who go right through today.

I want to raise that exercise with us, because it is the glad tidings of our salvation that is being presented to us, and we have the Holy Spirit of promise “who is the earnest of our inheritance”—the foretaste of the real thing. There is every inducement from the divine side to go on and not to remain in the wilderness; to enter into the purpose of God’s love, and to do so now.

Now, in Hebrews, Paul (I suppose the writer of this epistle) is addressing the Hebrew christians. We say that Hebrews is a wilderness epistle, and Paul presents to them what is heavenly. That is the purpose of God’s love for us—to enter into what is heavenly and to taste and experience the rest that we have sung about (Hymn 85). The promise is left of entering into His rest, and we are to fear lest any might seem to have failed of it. The promise will not fail, let us be sure of that God will not withdraw His promises. The opposition of the flesh in His people will never influence Him to withdraw His promises—they remain. But we may fail of them. That is a very serious consideration—to fail of the promise which He has left of entering into His rest.

Let me say that that is not ‘going to heaven when we die’, such as popular preaching holds out to people—something to be entered upon in the future. What God is presenting now to His people in the glad tidings of their salvation is to be entered into now; and we are responsible, and have the power, to do so. Every one who has received the Holy Spirit has the power in himself to enter into the purpose of God. So Caleb bore testimony to what kind of land it was, flowing with milk and honey, and he brought out the fruits of it, and he urged the people to go forward into it because, he said, “We are well able to do it” (Numbers 1: 30).

We need to regard ourselves, dear brethren, as those who have the Spirit and therefore have the power to enter in. Of course, the flesh is against the Spirit; it is lethargic, or it may be very active in opposition in any one of us. If this be so, we do not get the gain of the Spirit and may fail of the promise that is left us. But this epistle to the Hebrews is very stimulating, very encouraging to young people. The way to help young people is to encourage them.

Always put something before them to be reached, something to go on to. That is how Paul is writing this epistle, so that we do not settle down and remain on the wilderness side of Jordan, just enjoying the mercy of God and His providential care. That is a very attractive region to the flesh in us; not evil things, not gross things, but just comfortable, and suitable to settle down in, for flocks and herds. Some said they would go over Jordan and engage in the conflict, and they would come back again and dwell “on this side the Jordan eastward” (Numbers 32: 19). But the full thought of God is “the glad tidings of your salvation” and to go on into the fulness of the rest of God here.

So we find that God is referred to as swearing in His wrath as to certain who were not disposed to enter into His rest. They had had the word of the report, and what a report there has been from those who have gone this way! We have the ministry of such, who have gone into the land and brought us back the report and the evidence. How they have urged us to move on! It is a very necessary thing, if God gives us light, to see that the report is mixed with faith. That is really how faith comes. It comes by a report, and the report by God’s word (Romans 10: 17). It is God speaking in His word to us and we are tested as to our readiness to go forward.

It is very beautiful to see how God, having rested on the seventh day from all His works, desired man to enter into the enjoyment of rest. I do not think God secures much from restless persons. When we have been restless, God has not failed to minister comfort, the assurance of His interest, and many tokens of His mercy to us, day by day. But, in those conditions, He gets very little, if anything, from us.

How much the Lord had from Mary, who sat at His feet and was listening to His word! I wonder what the Lord was saying to Mary. I think He would have been opening up to her the depths of God. Do we want that? The depths of God are being searched by the Spirit of God, and He brings out things that men, as such, know nothing at all about. We want to accustom ourselves to do as Mary did. There she was, restful. We might say there are righteous obligations which we have to meet, but Mary somehow found time to sit down at the feet of Jesus and listen to His word. There was Martha, ‘bustling Martha’, she has been called, and she questioned His care. “Dost thou not care that my sister has left me to serve alone?” (Luke 10: 40). Well, Martha was adjusted, and she serves in restfulness, and there was more at Bethany for Christ in John 12 than there was for Him in Luke 10, much more, because there was what was collective and unified, and they were one in what was provided, in restfulness, for the heart of Christ.

So the rest remains, and God renews the opportunity for us to enter in. “Seeing therefore it remains that some enter into it, and those who first received the glad tidings did not enter in on account of not hearkening to the word, again he determines a certain day, saying, in David …” (Hebrews 4: 6, 7). God may have come to us before. He may have said something about this matter to us, and we may not have heeded it. Now He comes again. Think of God saying something in David to us, saying it in the true David, ‘great David’s greater Son’, saying “Today, after so long a time … today, if ye will hear his voice”. He gives us today—“as long as it is, called Today”, we read (Hebrews 3: 13). There is a little of the day left, so there is, time to commit ourselves in a fresh and vital way, to go on and to taste and experience what lies beyond death—a great order of things suited to God’s work, not only for us in the death of Jesus, but His work in us by the Spirit.

I do not know that I understand this verse fully—“Although the works had been completed from the foundation of the world” (Hebrews 4: 3). That is a long way back. The works have been completed. Think of the work of redemption, it has been completed. It was not an after-thought that God brought in. The works were completed from the foundation of the world.

The current of the Spirit’s mind is in the purpose of God—what has come out of eternity, and what is going into eternity. So Peter speaks of the blood of Christ, “foreknown indeed before the foundation of the world” (1 Peter 1: 20). Nothing has ever happened in the history of time that has caused God to modify His purpose. His purpose stands, according to election, as it says in Romans 9: 11.

Let me appeal to the elect, here in this little company tonight—the “elect according to the foreknowledge of God” (1 Peter 1: 2). God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world that we might receive sonship, for His praise and His glory, as we have in Ephesians 1: 12, “that we should be to the praise of his glory”. It is to such persons, elect according to the foreknowledge of God, the appeal comes, “Today, if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts”. Then, “Let us therefore use diligence”—be in the state of having used diligence—to enter into that rest, that no one may fall. It is not ‘fail’ here. Some might seem to have failed, but this is even more serious, to fall; it says “after the same example of not hearkening to the word”.

I would appeal to us, if God is urging in this direction, that we might not settle down, but go on to the full purpose of His love. Let us be those who use diligence, “for the word of God is living and operative”. It is God Himself “with whom we have to do”. I love the thought of having to do with God. He will have to do with all men. Here it is, Him “with whom we have to do”. We have had to do with Him today, and as long as He leaves us here we shall have to do with Him, but in love. It is very affecting that John writes to the little children, “because ye have known the Father” (1 John 2: 13). Do we know the Father? Let us, not put these things from us, thinking that they are beyond us.

Now I come to the passage in Matthew. It is quite clear that entering into rest here is not a matter of the future; it is present. The Lord says, “Come”. The Lord is addressing persons here who are burdened. He has spoken to the Father, and He speaks of the Father. Then He turns to those around Him and says, “Come to me, all ye who labour and are burdened, and I will give you rest”. It is very personal. He has to do with us individually and we have to come to Him to get what He has to dispense. “Come to me, all ye who labour and are burdened.”

How many are like that! How many are not fully in the liberty of the Spirit. The Lord says, “Take my yoke upon you”. That is a testing matter. If we desire to come into blessing, and into rest, it is upon the principle of relinquishing our wills.

How the Lord subdues us! The Lord can break a person’s will, if He has to do so. But what He desires to do is to subdue the will. Think of what He did to Saul of Tarsus. He could have crushed that man, but he rose up as a subdued man. His first word was, “Who art thou.

Lord?” Then, “What shall I do, Lord?” (Acts 22: 8, 10). That is a subdued person. That is the secret of progress in spiritual things, that you are subject to Christ, and that is the meaning of the yoke. It is a very intimate matter; it is identification with the rejected Christ here, because the cities had rejected Him and His ministry. At that very point it is said, “Jesus answering said, I praise thee, Father, Lord of the heaven and of the earth”; He is occupied in what is well-pleasing to the Father.

How wonderful the present moment is, this dispensation, that here in the presence of Satan’s power—so manifest in lawlessness rising up on every hand—that in the very midst of it there is a sphere where God is praised. That is what energised Mr. Darby as he began. He tells us, ‘I sought a place where God’s praises could be sung’, and he found a place. I trust we have found it. That a wonderful moment this is when, in spite of Satan’s power, the Father’s praises somewhere are being sung. We know where it is—“in the midst of the assembly will I sing thy praises” (Hebrews 2: 12). This is the great assembly gospel, Matthew; and the way into the assembly is to be subject to Christ. “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me”; that is, the Lord is taking on this matter of instruction. He is taking on persons to instruct them, to make them disciples. “Learn from me”—He is not deputing the teaching to anyone else; He does it Himself. Oh, it is a great thing to come to Christ in subduedness of spirit and to learn from Him. He says, “I am meek and lowly in heart, and ye shall find rest to your souls”.

Much was said a few years ago about the sabbath, and we found ourselves on Jewish ground; but “There remains then a sabbatism to the people of God” (Hebrews 4: 9). You say, Where is it? The question is not only, Where is it? but Who is it?—Jesus is the rest of God, the One who says here, “Come to me … and I will give you rest … and ye shall find rest to your souls; for my yoke is easy, and my burden is light”. I think we shall find, in company with Him, how quickly the transit is made from the plains of Moab to the things which Paul speaks of as “the glad tidings of your salvation”. May we know it increasingly, for His name’s sake.

“MY HIGH PLACES”—We may learn a lesson from the blackbird. Morning and night he loves to perch on the highest point of a tree and pour out his song. For a believer, too, it is a good thing to resort to his highest point and let his soul go out to God in response. In an evil, day, Habakkuk speaks of “my high places” (Habakkuk 3: 19). We are to have our high places, and God delights to hear our song of praise from them.
“SET … BY HIM”—When the disciples reasoned who should be the greatest of them, “Jesus ... having taken a little child set it by him”, (Luke 9: 47). That place may be yours and mine.

Could you want a better place? You may be as near to Him as you wish; have as much of His company as you desire. Would that little child have the slightest interest in the discussion as to who should be greatest? It would be wholly content, and that contentedness would preclude all ambition and rivalry.

SKILL AND FERVOUR—“Play skilfully with a loud sound” (Psalm 33: 3). The Spirit would delight to make us skilled in the service of God, to be marked by refinement of spiritual feeling, and to be able to contribute to the fine harmonies of the greatest of all services. But along with skill is to go fervour, holy exuberance—and outpouring of soul. So the service is spontaneous and is to move the depths of our beings as we call upon all that is within us to bless God (Psalm 103: 1).
